name: The Paradox of Tragedy
aliases: The paradox of negative emotion in art
statement: Why do we seek out and enjoy art that makes us feel sorrow, fear, and distress?
statementAccent: art that makes us feel sorrow, fear, and distress
meaning: The paradox of tragedy is the puzzle of why audiences find pleasure or satisfaction in tragic art, dramas, novels, films, and music that depict suffering, death, and misfortune and arouse painful, negative emotions such as pity, fear, sorrow, and distress. Why do we seek out and enjoy works that make us feel bad, and how can painful emotions be part of a pleasurable and valued aesthetic experience? The puzzle is often framed as a set of jointly inconsistent claims: that appreciating tragic art involves a negatively valenced, distressing state; that we do not, in general, pursue experiences for the distress they cause; and yet that we do pursue and take pleasure in tragic art. A broader version covers other negative emotions in art, including the paradox of horror discussed by Noel Carroll. The puzzle has a long history. Aristotle, in the Poetics, held that tragedy arouses pity and fear and accomplishes their catharsis, often read as part of an answer. David Hume, in his 1757 essay Of Tragedy, asked why spectators receive an unaccountable pleasure from the sorrow, terror, and anxiety of a well-written tragedy, and offered a conversion theory on which the force of the painful passions is converted into pleasure by the eloquence and artistry of the representation. Modern solutions include compensation and control theories, and Susan Feagin's distinction between our direct response to tragic events and our positive meta-response of pleasure at our own compassionate reaction.
mechanism: The paradox arises because tragic art seems to give pleasure precisely through emotions that are, in themselves, unpleasant. A theory must explain how the sorrow and fear a tragedy arouses can be sought out and enjoyed rather than avoided. Aristotle's catharsis is one traditional line: tragedy arouses pity and fear and then works on them, whether by purging, purifying, or clarifying them, so that the audience gains relief, refinement, or understanding, though what catharsis means is famously disputed. Hume's conversion theory locates the resolution in the art itself: the very qualities that make a tragedy painful in content, the vivid representation of sorrow and terror, are handled with such eloquence, imitation, and beauty that the predominant movement of the beautiful expression converts the subordinate painful passion into pleasure, so that spectators are, as Hume put it, pleased in proportion as they are afflicted, the artistry transforming the pain. Modern compensation theories hold that we undergo the painful emotions for the sake of some sufficiently valuable good that outweighs or offsets them, whether the formal and artistic pleasures of the work, hedonic compensation, or the cognitive and moral goods of understanding, insight, and meaning, non-hedonic compensation. Control theories add that our awareness that we can direct our engagement, that the events are represented rather than real and that we can look away, mitigates the aversive character of the emotions and lets us dwell on them safely. Susan Feagin's account, from her 1983 paper, distinguishes a negative direct response to the tragic events from a positive meta-response, a pleasure taken in discovering that we are the kind of people who respond to villainy and suffering with the right compassionate feelings.

examples.text: Hume held the artistry of a tragedy converts the painful passions into pleasure, so we are pleased in proportion as we are afflicted.
We undergo painful emotions for the sake of compensating goods, whether artistic pleasure or cognitive and moral insight.
Feagin distinguished a negative response to the events from a positive pleasure at finding ourselves to respond compassionately.

variants.name: Conversion versus compensation
variants.text: Hume's transformation of pain into pleasure by artistry, versus modern theories of offsetting goods that outweigh the pain.

variants.name: Direct and meta-responses
variants.text: Feagin's distinction between the first-order distress at tragic events and the second-order pleasure at one's own compassion.

whyItMatters: The paradox of tragedy is a central problem in aesthetics and the philosophy of emotion, because it strikes at a puzzling but pervasive fact about the value of art: that some of the most esteemed and sought-after works, tragedies, sad songs, harrowing films, deliberately arouse painful emotions, and audiences prize them for it. Explaining this forces us to think about the nature of the emotions, about the relation between the content of an artwork and our response to it, and about what we get from art that could justify undergoing distress for its sake. The problem has a distinguished lineage, from Aristotle's catharsis and Hume's elegant conversion theory to the compensation, control, and meta-response accounts of contemporary aesthetics, and it connects to a family of related puzzles, the paradox of horror and the broader paradox of negative emotion in art, as well as to the paradox of fiction. It bears directly on the question of why art matters and what it offers us, since a good answer must identify the goods, emotional, cognitive, moral, or aesthetic, that make painful art worthwhile.

working.text: observe that tragic art deliberately arouses painful feelings such as pity, fear, and sorrow.
recognize that we nonetheless seek out and enjoy such art, contrary to our aversion to distress.
explain the pleasure through catharsis, the conversion of pain by artistry, compensating goods, or a positive meta-response.

limits: The paradox of tragedy is a genuine problem admitting several competing solutions rather than a settled result, and each solution has limits. Aristotle's catharsis, often invoked, is itself obscure and disputed, since Aristotle never clearly explains it, so it is more a placeholder than a worked-out answer. Hume's conversion theory is challenged to say exactly how the pleasure of artistry converts rather than merely accompanies or outweighs the pain, and whether conversion is the right model at all. Compensation theories must specify the compensating goods and explain why they require the painful emotions rather than being obtainable without them, and control theories must say how mere awareness of representation dampens genuine distress. Feagin's meta-response account is questioned as to whether the pleasure really attaches to our own compassion rather than to the work, and whether it covers all cases. A further worry is whether the negative emotions aroused by tragedy are painful in quite the way ordinary distress is. Some attributions and datings reward care: Hume's Of Tragedy is dated 1757, Feagin's paper 1983, and Carroll's paradox of horror 1990.
misreadings: The paradox of tragedy is not the claim that audiences enjoy suffering as such; the puzzle is that a valued pleasure arises through, not in spite of, painful emotions artfully aroused. Catharsis is not an agreed solution, since its meaning is disputed and Aristotle never explained it. And the pleasure of tragedy need not mean the negative emotions are secretly pleasant, since the leading theories transform, compensate, or reframe them, so treating the paradox as enjoyment of suffering, as solved by catharsis, or as showing the emotions are really pleasant, misreads it.
origin: The puzzle, treated by Aristotle's catharsis and Hume's 1757 essay Of Tragedy and developed by modern compensation, control, and meta-response theories, of why audiences seek out and enjoy tragic art that arouses painful emotions.
